source.title: The Fragility of Jailbreak Robustness Across Operational States
source.authors: Yuna Park; Hwang Youn Kim; Yujin Kim; Won Woo Ro; Suhyun Kim; Jae-In Hwang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites the single-direction refusal finding and uses a learned refusal-related representation axis to analyze jailbreak outcomes. It does not test the original difference-in-means direction or intervene on it.
record.gate_note: The paper measures associations between a logistic-regression axis trained to distinguish jailbreak success from failure and jailbreak outcomes. It does not test the original direction by ablating or adding it, test weight edits, or measure whether attacks suppress that direction. The reported state-conditioned ASRs do not establish the direction mechanism. Accordingly, no claim version is tested; axis-related results are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Arditi et al. as motivation, then trains its own logistic-regression axis on jailbreak success vs. failure labels (not a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means). It reports only correlations between projection and ASR, with no ablation, addition or weight edit. It therefore measures a related but different construct, a predictive probe of jailbreak outcome. It tests no version, including V3, since it never shows attacks suppress the original direction.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The main conclusion is that ordinary, safety-irrelevant system prompts can greatly change jailbreak ASR for a fixed attack (e.g. 2%→58% for Llama-2-7B under LAA), so single vanilla-state evaluation is insufficient. They propose an SSI stability metric. The representation result is presented as predictive only, explicitly without establishing a causal role for the axis.
record.recipe_differences: The original uses a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction and intervenes by ablating or adding it. This paper instead trains a logistic-regression axis to distinguish jailbreak success from failure and reports predictive associations without causal interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Projection–ASR association is reported across layers and prompt-set splits; the paper notes that predictive performance is higher when training and evaluation use the same prompt family.

fits_no_version.finding: In Llama-2-7B/13B-chat under LAA, a linear probe on final pre-generation token states predicts jailbreak success (AUROC 0.89–0.98). Mean projection per system-prompt state tracks state ASR (r 0.61–0.98). No causal test is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign system-prompt (persona) states shift hidden states along a linear axis that predicts jailbreak success, in step with the state's ASR.

record.problems: The representation analysis is primarily on one model and attack, with 50 queries for the main operational-state analysis. The learned axis is trained to classify jailbreak success versus failure rather than refusal from harmful-versus-harmless instructions, and no causal intervention is performed. The authors also note that performance is higher within prompt families and that the probe may capture prompt-family-specific artifacts.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's system-prompt-conditioned jailbreak ASR results, including the main model-by-attack tables, are not included because they do not measure or intervene on the refusal direction. Other attack-success state comparisons and harm-category results likewise do not test a listed claim version.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction, no ablation or addition, no capability check.
No test of whether attacks suppress the refusal direction, and no adversarial training against its ablation. The learned axis is a success/failure probe, and its link to ASR is correlational only.
No single-direction versus multi-direction, affine or cone comparison.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
No transfer of the original direction. The Llama-2-7B replication retrains its own probe.
No comparison of training procedures or stages.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's gate is right. The axis is supervised on jailbreak outcome labels, so its correlation with ASR partly follows from how it was built. The authors also flag prompt-family artifacts. The ASR tables (Table 9 etc.) are correctly left out, since they measure no direction.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means harmful-minus-harmless direction, all-layer/position ablation, direction addition, or general-capability check.
No refusal-direction weight edit or abliteration evaluation.
The paper does not test whether attacks suppress the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
No comparison of single-direction, affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No transfer test of the original refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
No comparison of refusal training procedures or training stages.

rows.subject: Llama-2-13B-chat-hf
rows.operation_detail: A logistic-regression probe trained to distinguish jailbreak success from failure; mean hidden-state projection across operational states was related to ASR.

conditions.value: vanilla and five Big Five states

rows.measure: Pearson correlation between mean projection and state ASR
rows.uncertainty: p = 0.005; horizontal error bars are standard errors
rows.note: The learned axis is described as refusal-related, but is trained on jailbreak success/failure labels, not harmful-versus-harmless instructions. The association does not establish causality.
